1:
Only Ellicott gives the "wherefore" a history. The teaching just laid down "brings the Gentiles up to the same level with the Jews", so the vices are a party quarrel: "ill will put into action... on the part of these Hebrew Christians against their Gentile brethren", with guile, hypocrisies and jealousies as "instances of concealed malice". He sorts them by function — "the first plots, the second pretends not to plot, and the third rejoices to think of the plot succeeding" — and renders the last item literally as "all talkings down". Calvin takes the connective back to the new birth: "it is not sufficient for us to have been once called by the Lord, except we live as new creatures."

Robertson says the verb for laying aside can mean cleansing defilement or taking off clothes, and will not choose: "either sense suits here". Gill has chosen: the vices are "old worn out clothes, as filthy rags... never used more", and Ellicott, quoting Leighton, "ragged filthy habits, unbeseeming the children of God".

Henry narrows malice to "settled overgrown anger, retained till it inflames a man to design mischief", and splits hypocrisy: "in matters of religion hypocrisy is counterfeit piety. In civil conversation hypocrisy is counterfeit friendship." Wesley adds that dissimulation "is the outward expression of guile in the heart". Robertson notes hypocrisies is singular "in the best MSS", the fourth word envies, "not murders, as B has it".

On the babes they divide over the newness. Ellicott insists on "newly, lately born, not born anew", the name fitting because "they are still so far from maturity in Christ, as these sins testified". Gill makes it universal: even "those of the longest standing were but as it were newly born". Robertson notes the adjective alludes to the verb for being born again in the previous chapter, so "they were recent converts".

What kind of milk is the sharpest disagreement. Calvin rejects Erasmus's "milk not for the body but for the soul" and pairs the two adjectives deliberately: "simplicity and quickness of understanding are two things apparently opposite; but they ought to be mixed together, lest simplicity should become insipid, and lest malicious craftiness should creep in." Barnes reads it as "properly rational, pertaining to reason", finding two ideas: that "the proper aliment of piety is simple truth", and that these were "the more elementary truths of the gospel". Ellicott is flatly negative: the English "of the word" "cannot possibly be right". Robertson lays the alternatives side by side without deciding — "the milk belonging to the word", or "rational or spiritual" as in Romans — and gives the second adjective its edge: unadulterated milk "which, alas, is so hard to get". Clarke hears a rabbinic register, learning the law being called sucking and disciples "those that suck the breast", and argues for adding unto salvation at the verse's end on ABC "and about forty others" — the reading "undoubtedly genuine, and is very important".

The last clause is a quotation, and the argument concerns a tense and a letter. Ellicott would render it "ye tasted", looking back to the first conversion, "when the taste of spiritual things is the most delicious. How sad to be past the relish for evangelical truth!" He disowns the English adjective, adopted "to suit the Prayer Book version of the Psalm" but "scarcely suitable to the Greek word", running from serviceable to whatever is mild and pleasant. Clarke reports that many manuscripts and several fathers read Christ for gracious, "from the similarity of the letters". Barnes and Wesley read the conditional as a statement: "since you have tasted."

Ellicott alone draws the doctrinal consequence: Peter applies to Christ a passage "which otherwise we might not have thought of applying to Him in particular", which "gives quite a new complexion to the 34th Psalm". Robertson makes the taste a beginning: "a taste excites the appetite."
4:
Two commentators find the phrase deliberately impossible. Robertson finds "an apparent intentional contradiction between living and stone", of a piece with the living hope and living word earlier; Barnes admits the difficulty rather than resolving it, calling the phrase "unusual, and is not found, I think, except in this place. There seems to be an incongruity in it, in attributing life to a stone" — the point being that no temple of "gold and costly stones" is meant but "a temple composed of living materials", redeemed men.

Henry hears the metaphor as its first readers would. To "a capricious wit, or an infidel, this description may seem rough and harsh", but to Jews "who placed much of their religion in their magnificent temple, and who understood the prophetical style", it "would appear very elegant and proper". Ellicott registers the same shift: from here the regeneration imagery of the first chapter "suddenly disappears", and the thought becomes "that of a spiritual Temple instead of the stone temple at Jerusalem".

Whether Peter is thinking of his own name divides them sharply. Gill takes the verse as a disclaimer — Peter "shows that he is not the rock, but Christ is the rock on which the church is built" — and Wesley agrees that in speaking thus he "did not judge himself, but Christ, to be the rock on which the church was built". Ellicott calls it "more than doubtful", arguing from vocabulary: the word here is neither petros nor petra but lithos, and neither of the first two "could possibly be used of the squared wrought stone", both meaning the native unhewn substratum that exists before any building begins.

He also finds the order significant — "the very structure and order of the sentence puts Jesus Christ first. Foundation first, building afterwards" — and objects to the English supplement: "it is a pity to insert as unto with our version; it takes off from the striking, attracting effect of the sudden metaphor." The participle for coming is the verb behind proselyte: "joining Him therefore as proselytes."

What the coming is gets a second answer. Gill denies it is conversion at all: it "does not design the first act of faith on Christ, or a soul's first coming to Christ, but an after and continued exercise of faith on him". Calvin makes it the effect of the taste just mentioned, since "the human mind necessarily dreads and shuns God, as long as it regards him as rigid and severe", but once his paternal love is known men "forget themselves and hasten to him" — so that "he only makes progress in the Gospel, who in heart comes to God".

The rejection is handled as a pastoral problem, not only a fact. Calvin sees the danger that Christ might "be despised by us" because he is widely despised, and answers that "he, notwithstanding, retains his own worth and honor before God". Wesley extends the list of rejecters past the obvious: not only "Jews, Turks, heathens, infidels; but by all Christians, so called, who live in sin, or who hope to be saved by their own works". Clarke draws the opposite conclusion from the choosing: "God can never be mistaken in his choice; therefore he that chooses Christ for his portion shall never be confounded."

Robertson supplies the words that carry the contrast. The verb for rejection means "to repudiate after test"; the balancing phrase is spatial, "by the side of God, as he looks at it"; and the adjective is not the proved one that test-word leads you to expect but precious, "a pre-eminence of position with" God. Clarke translates it "honourable" and extends the honour to the building, since those united to him "partake of the same honor" — the stones of a building being "of no use but as they occupy their proper places".
5:
Two commentators want the English changed. Barnes says the word should have been rendered living, "lively with us now" having "a different meaning from living" and denoting "active, quick, sprightly"; Ellicott calls the variation "arbitrary, the Greek being precisely the same", the repetition serving "to show the complete conformation of the believers to Him who is the type and model for humanity".

Gill notes the metaphor was not Peter's invention: poets called stones "living" while they lay in the quarry, and he cites Virgil's vivoque sedilia saxo. His own use of it is sharper: saints "lie in the same quarry, and are the same by nature as the rest of mankind, till dug out and separated from thence by the powerful and efficacious grace of God".

Whether the verb is a statement or a command is undecidable, and both say so. Calvin observes that "the termination in Greek is ambiguous", so it "may be in the imperative as well as in the indicative mood", though either way Peter "meant to exhort the faithful to consecrate themselves as a spiritual temple to God". Ellicott agrees "the one is as grammatical as the other" and prefers the command, suiting "the hortatory character of the whole Epistle".

Clarke faces the objection nobody else raises: "what analogy is there between the stones of a building and a multitude of human beings?" His answer is philological. In Hebrew the words for house, son, daughter and stone all stand on one root meaning he built, so a house is built of stones as a household is made of sons and daughters — the analogy is in the language before it is in the figure.

The house is emphatically one house. Calvin insists that "though every one of us is said to be the temple of God, yet all are united together in one, and must be joined together by mutual love, so that one temple may be made of us all" — which happens when "every one, content with his own measure, keeps himself within the limits of his own duty". Robertson reads the same corporate sense out of the verb Jesus used to Peter about building his church, concluding Peter understood that saying "to be not a local church, but the church general". Of the priesthood he says Peter holds that "all believers are priests and can approach God directly". Ellicott adds what it is chiefly for: "not in its capacity of a place for worship so much as a place for Divine inhabitation" — Leighton's "palace of the Great King".

The quotation is introduced with a textual correction. Ellicott holds "the right reading here is not wherefore also, but because", and presses the odd verb — the passage "encloses or contains" the words — drawing "attention to the context of the quotation". He reports the exegetical history: on Gesenius's evidence the early Jewish reading referred Isaiah's stone to the Messiah, while "the later Rabbinical expositors, probably by way of opposition to the Christians, explained it to mean Hezekiah". Gill comes at it from the other end, the Targum applying it to a mighty king without naming him, "but Jarchi expressly names him".

Robertson notes the term for chief corner stone was "apparently invented by Isaiah", and where Isaiah's metaphor "is rather a foundation stone", Peter and Paul make it "the primary foundation stone at the structure". Clarke locates it at the angle "where its two sides form the ground work of a side and end wall", and draws the inference: in Jesus "both Jews and Gentiles were to be united". He and Barnes both note the Hebrew of the closing promise reads "shall not make haste", which Clarke turns into consolation — the believer "need not haste to flee away, for no enemy shall ever be able to annoy him". Wesley adds two words: "in time or in eternity."
7:
The verse turns on three words of English. The Authorised Version reads "he is precious"; the margin reads "an honour"; the commentators split. Barnes defends the text and rejects the margin — believing on Christ is indeed an honour, "but it is very doubtful whether this is the idea of Peter", since "the apostle was not showing that it was an honour to believe on Christ, but was stating the estimate which was put on him by those who believe, as contrasted with the view taken of him by the world". The noun, he grants, is properly "esteem, honour, respect, reverence... then value or price", but "the connexion demands this interpretation".

Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all take the other side. Clarke renders it "the honor is to you who believe", meaning "the honor of being in this building, and of having your souls saved through the blood of the Lamb". Robertson glosses the noun as "the preciousness" or "the honour" and makes it the explanation of the words just quoted from Isaiah. Ellicott rests the case on the contrast: both Hebrew and Greek "may with equal propriety be translated honoured, and this contrasts better with the shame just spoken of", and he cites an earlier authority for it.

Ellicott then lays out the argument in a paraphrase. "God has selected Jesus for special honour, and has promised that all who trust in Him, instead of scorning Him like the Jewish rulers, shall have no cause to blush. Now you do trust in Him, therefore to you belongs the promise, and the honour bestowed by God on Him reflects on you. You, like Him, are made parts of the divine imperishable architecture." Calvin reaches the same inference by a shorter road: "Christ is a precious stone in the sight of God; then he is such to the faithful" — because "it is faith alone which reveals to us the value and excellency of Christ."

Ellicott adds a second textual point: "the better reading is, Unto them which disbelieve", the word in our text "being an importation from" the following verse, and the true reading "better preserves the contrast with you that believe". He also notices what Peter does not say. One expects the sentence to run on to the shame the unbelievers incur; instead "the Apostle stops short, and inserts (by a quotation) the historical fact which brought the shame".

Robertson traces that quotation through its uses. It comes from the psalm with an allusion back to Isaiah; Jesus quoted it to apply the builders' rejection — "the experts" — to the Sanhedrin's conduct toward him; Peter had quoted it the same way at the Beautiful Gate, and "here he quotes it again to the same purpose". Calvin draws out the two things the verse asserts: that Christ "was rejected by those who bore rule in the Church of God", and that "their efforts were all in vain".

Gill spends his space on who the believers are not. Not "all they that can say their creed, or give their assent to the articles of it"; not all who believe a divine revelation; not all who believe the whole Gospel and every truth in it; nor "all that say they believe, or profess to do so" — but only those "who have seen themselves lost and undone by sin, their need of a Saviour". Barnes argues from evidence rather than definition: Christians "perceive a value in him which is seen in nothing else", avowing him "their best friend".

Wesley and Clarke both let the rejected keep the stone. Clarke: "that very person whom they reject is head of the corner — is Lord over all, and has all power in the heavens and the earth." Wesley makes the same point prospectively, that unbelievers "too will at length find him such to their sorrow".
8:
The figure changes completely, and Ellicott insists on it: "there is no thought whatever of the stone as a material for building; the thought is that of a mass of rock on the road, on which the terror-stricken fugitives stumble and fall." He reads it out of Isaiah's Immanuel section, where the stone is sanctuary to one party and obstacle to the other — not a temple but "such a sanctuary as that of Bethel, a consecrated stone to which a man might flee as an asylum", which in the flight before the Assyrians became "a vexatious and dangerous obstacle" to those who did not trust it.

He also accuses the Greek Old Testament. Peter translates from the Hebrew, because the Septuagint "not only makes nonsense, but can again be hardly acquitted of guile in its endeavour to make out the best possible case for Israel by deliberately inserting the word not twice over". On the pairing of the quotations he grants a Pauline look but reverses the dependence: Peter "must have been present and heard the Lord of Hosts Himself put them together", Paul tracing "back to the same origin".

The two nouns are distinguished, then un-distinguished. Robertson says the first "is an obstacle against which one strikes by accident, while" the second "is a trap set to trip one, but both make one fall", adding that "too much distinction need not be made" between a loose stone and a ledge in the ground. Barnes takes the second word back to its origin: "a trap-stick — a crooked stick on which the bait is fastened, which the animal strikes against, and so springs the trap". It is "not a matter of indifference whether they believe on him or not".

Why they stumbled is answered twice. Gill catalogues the offences — the virgin birth, the meanness of his parents, the education that made them ask "how he should know letters", and "the obscurity of his kingdom". Clarke names one cause instead, and not the usual one: the Gospel "called the Gentiles to be a peculiar people whom the Jews believed to be everlastingly reprobated" — "the true cause why the Jews rejected the Gospel".

Calvin keeps the fault off Christ, whose "proper office is to prepare us for a spiritual temple to God; but it is the fault of men that they stumble at him", so that "as he has been given to us as a foundation, it is as it were an accidental thing that he becomes a rock of offense". He turns the charge on his own age: "the Papists do the same in the present day; they worship only the name of Christ, while they cannot endure the doctrine of the Gospel."

The last clause divides them four ways. Calvin lays out both senses — appointed to believe, since "the promise of salvation was destined for them", or "appointed to unbelief; as Pharaoh is said to have been set up for this end" — inclining to the second on the strength of a particle, and taking the antecedent to be the stumbling itself. Robertson keeps the ordination narrow, quoting Bigg: "their disobedience is not ordained, the penalty of their disobedience is." Ellicott makes it prophetic rather than causal: Peter "primarily means that the clear prophecies of the Old Testament which he has quoted marked them for such a destiny", it being "no unforeseen, accidental consequence of the gospel". Wesley states it hardest: "God having appointed from all eternity, he that believeth not shall be damned."

Clarke escapes by re-punctuating: following Macknight he carries the sense forward from the preceding verse, "the disobedient stumble against the word, or doctrine, to which verily they were appointed". Ellicott rearranges within the verse: better "which stumble, being disobedient to the word", the participle explaining the verb, "the manner of the stumbling" being "in being disobedient to the gospel preaching".
9:
Every title is borrowed, and they agree on the source before disagreeing about who inherits. Clarke sets them out from Deuteronomy and Exodus, observing that titles "formerly given to the whole Jewish Church... are here given to Christians in general in the same way". Calvin turns the borrowing into a warning: "Moses called formerly your fathers a holy nation, a priestly kingdom, and God's peculiar people: all these high titles do now far more justly belong to you; therefore you ought to beware lest your unbelief should rob you of them" — the fathers having had "an earthly taste only".

Ellicott presses the first title into a doctrine of the church. As Abraham's clan was chosen from all the families of the earth, "so out of the clan of Abraham after the flesh were these men selected to be a new clan, or race": not "individuals selected one by one and left in isolation, but a tribe consolidated". Gill takes the kinship three ways: akin to God as Father, to Christ as head and brother, and to one another as one household.

On royal Ellicott is precise and unexpected. The word "does not seem intended to imply that every Christian is a king", but "describes his belonging to the King as we might speak of the royal apartments, the royal borough, or even of the royal servants". The substitution of priesthood for Exodus's priests is compensation: "if the writer had said royal priests, the notion of organisation would have slipped out of sight altogether." Barnes prefers Doddridge's reading, that they "at once bore the dignity of kings, and the sanctity of priests".

Both draw the same conclusion for church order. Ellicott notes that the words "describe the whole Israelite nation as they stood beneath Mount Sinai", so "the sacerdotal office was as common to all Israelites under the Law as it is to all the new Israel under the Gospel" — which "must be taken into consideration in dealing with the doctrine of the Christian ministry". Robertson states it flatly: the officer in Christian churches is presbyter-overseer, not priest; "we are all priests."

The fourth title gets the closest philology. Ellicott renders it "a people for a special reservation", matching neither the Greek nor the Hebrew of Exodus. Robertson defends the old English: "the old rendering, a peculiar people, had this idea of possession." The noun for praises he calls an "old word for any preeminence (moral, intellectual, military)", though in the Isaiah quoted "it means praise and glory to God". Darkness he glosses as heathenism, the marvellous light as Christianity.

Who these people were before is answered four ways. Clarke says they "had been Gentiles, covered with ignorance and superstition". Barnes says the passage "refers mainly to those who had been Gentiles, and who had never been recognised as the people of God", adding that Peter's use of Hosea is "a mere allusion... without meaning to say that both refer to the same subject". Wesley splits the verse: "the former part... particularly respects the gentiles; the latter, the Jews." Calvin reads it of the Jews first, scattered "as the torn members of a body" and so "repudiated by the Lord" — granting that Paul applies the prophecy to the Gentiles "not without reason", since once the covenant was broken "they were put on a level with the Gentiles".

Ellicott treats the verse as evidence and rejects the obvious inference. Some take it for "a distinct proof that the Epistle was written to the Gentiles only", but "such, however, is by no means the case; in fact, the opposite" — the unpitied and rejected in Hosea being Israel itself, restored "together with the increment of the Gentiles who joined it". Robertson quotes Hort on the tense, moving from "the long antecedent state" to "the single event of conversion which ended it".
11:
Whether the two words are literal or figurative is the first dispute. Clarke takes them at face value: these "were strangers and pilgrims in the most literal sense of the word", scattered through Asia and Pontus. Calvin denies it — Peter calls them so "not because they were banished from their country, and scattered into various lands, but because the children of God, wherever they may be, are only guests in this world" — and Ellicott agrees the word is here "used in a metaphorical and not literal sense".

The English word pilgrim is then disowned. Ellicott says it "does not originally, or in this place, mean one on a pilgrimage. It implies no journeying, but simply residence in a foreign country." Barnes had defined it the other way, "one who travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place... then a traveller, a wanderer". Wesley splits them by scale: "the first word properly means, those who are in a strange house; the second, those who are in a strange country."

Ellicott traces the pair to the psalm, where they "prepare for the description of distress which is to follow", and quotes Leighton: "it is because I love you that I intreat you... as you love yourselves, to abstain from fleshly lusts." Gill hears the same tone: Peter does not "in an authoritative way command, as he might have done, as an apostle, but, as a friend, he entreats". Henry adds the uncomfortable inference: "even the best of men... need to be exhorted to keep from the worst sins."

Calvin widens what is forbidden: the phrase covers "not only those gross concupiscences which we have in common with animals, as the Sophists hold, but also all those sinful passions and affections of the soul". Robertson keeps it narrow, "the grosser sins of the flesh". Clarke makes the picture vivid: the lusts are "marshalled and drawn up in battle array, to fight against the soul; either to slay it, or to bring it into captivity".

The word rendered honest defeats all three who try it. Ellicott: "we have no word adequate to represent this charming adjective"; it is "the ordinary Greek word for beautiful, and implies the attractiveness of the sight". Calvin: "neither conversation nor honest are suitable words... perhaps life would be the best word." Robertson renders the later phrase as a result: "out of your good (beautiful) deeds".

Why the warning was needed is explained historically. Clarke observes that in the first age "the Christians and the Jews were confounded together" abroad, so Christians "shared in their blame". Calvin says the same from the other side: the Jews "were not only hated everywhere, but were also almost abhorred", and had the more to "wipe off the odium and infamy attached to their name". Robertson puts it as surveillance: "the Gentiles are on the watch for slips in moral conduct by the Christians."

Barnes lays out the two constructions of whereas and refuses to arbitrate — temporal, so that at the very time they slander you they are silenced, or "in respect to which" — since "the question which is meant is not very important". Ellicott prefers the margin and finds a use for the slander itself: "the very fact of the heathen having slandered them will make their testimony in the day of visitation all the more striking", as Thomas's doubts tend "to the more confirmation of the faith".

The day of visitation is read three ways. Clarke makes it judgment, "when God should come to execute judgment on the disobedient Jews, in the destruction of their civil polity". Wesley makes it mercy: "the time when he shall give them fresh offers of his mercy." Henry keeps both open, a day "wherein God may call to repentance by his word and his grace". Robertson notes a "clear echo here of" the Sermon on the Mount.
13:
The phrase is literally "every human creation", and nobody is content with the English. Clarke says the words "literally signify, not every ordinance of man, but every human creature", but since the verb can also mean to arrange, "it is better to understand the words thus, All the constituted authorities". Gill takes the creature to be the heathen magistrate, created and installed as such. Calvin gets a doctrine of society out of the verb, which means to construct a building: "God the maker of the world has not left the human race in a state of confusion, that they might live after the manner of beasts, but as it were in a building regularly formed" — the arrangement called human "not because it has been invented by man, but because a mode of living, well arranged and duly ordered, is peculiar to men".

Ellicott sets the verse against its Pauline model and finds the reasoning reversed. In Romans the ground of submission is that "the authority proceeds from God Himself"; here "the thought is quite different. They are to submit... because of the practical consequences of not submitting" — for the Lord's sake, "in order not to bring discredit upon His teaching, and persecution upon His Church". The difference he explains by circumstance: Paul urged submission to Claudius because Roman Jews were being expelled, Peter because "ignorant and foolish men" were beginning to misrepresent the Church "as a kind of Internationalist or Socialist conspiracy". Wesley keeps both grounds in a line: "instrumentally these are ordained by men; but originally all their power is from God."

Calvin adds the Jewish side: they were "counted infamous... because they were regarded on account of their perverseness as ungovernable", while among Christians "many thought the gospel was a proclamation of such liberty, that every one might deem himself as free from servitude" — the magistrates being besides "Christ's adversaries".

How far the submission goes is where they part. Barnes enters the usual limitation, that what is ordained be "not contrary to the law of God"; Ellicott warns that Peter "does not say we are to submit to every law that men may pass"; Robertson agrees he "approves no special kind of government, but he supports law and order" unless it "steps in between God and man". Clarke alone allows no such reservation in practice: "genuine Christians have nothing to do with the laws but to obey them. Society and civil security are in a most dangerous state when the people take it into their heads that they have a right to remodel and change the laws." Henry draws the distinction that softens the question: magistracy "is certainly of divine right; but the particular form of government, the power of the magistrate, and the persons who are to execute this power, are of human institution".

Ellicott notes that "the name king, though detested in Latin, was used without scruple by the provincial Greeks", and that supreme does not contrast the emperor with the governors, since "the emperor was in the Roman Empire not merely the highest, but actually the only ruler". Who sends those governors is a flat disagreement. Ellicott says "the person by whom they are here said to be sent is Cæsar, not the Lord"; Robertson says "by God, as Jesus made plain to Pilate", who received his authority from above. Ellicott adds an illustration of how personal that government was: in Pliny's correspondence "the very letter before that in which he asks how to deal with the Christians of Bithynia requests Trajan's leave to cover in an unhealthy beck".

What they are for is agreed. Ellicott credits Roman imperialism, "rightly in the main", with aiming at "the promotion of moral behaviour among its subjects"; Barnes quotes Ulpian on a president's duty to keep his province quiet. Calvin concludes there is "no kind of government to which we ought not to submit".
15:
The verb behind "put to silence" is the one used of animals, and three press it. Clarke renders it "to muzzle, i.e., stop their mouths, leave them nothing to say; let them assert, but ever be unable to bring proof". Calvin admits the phrase "to stop up ignorance" "may seem harsh on account of its novelty", but keeps the image, "according to what is done to savage animals, in order to prevent them to do harm". Ellicott finds contempt everywhere — the muzzling implies "there is something of the animal about these foolish men", and even men "might be rendered people or creatures". Robertson notes the alliteration.

Wesley breaks with that tone entirely. The ignorance is that "of them who blame you, because they do not know you: a strong motive to pity them." Barnes stands between: the accusers were foolish "in the sense of evil-disposed, or wicked", yet "though there might be malice at the bottom, the charges were really based on ignorance". Calvin turns the epithet into an argument: Peter "points out the reason why they slandered, even because they were ignorant of God", whence "a right understanding cannot exist without the knowledge of God".

Ellicott reads the next phrase as the heart of the charge. "The Christian took up a position of complete independence within, and professed himself in a certain sense to be above the laws, by virtue of being a member of Christ's kingdom. This position the heathen state resented, and looked upon the Christian Church as a dangerous organisation." Peter therefore "both insists upon, and defines that independent position", warning against dreaming of "an exemption from obedience".

The historical form of the abuse is Jewish. Barnes notes that the Jews "never willingly acknowledged their subjection to any other power", holding "that God only was their Sovereign", and that Josephus records rebellions raised on that plea. Clarke says flatly that "they used their liberty for a cloak of maliciousness — for a pretext of rebellion". Gill keeps the freedom real but bounded: they were "Christ's freemen, free from sin... but then they were not free to sin".

Calvin generalises — at the beginning of the Gospel "many thought themselves free to live only for themselves" — and gives the definition the tile turns on: "true liberty, then, is that which harms or injures no one." Robertson makes the point negatively: "there is no such thing as absolute freedom... for that is anarchy", and notes that the closing title, bondservants of God, is "Paul's proud title".

How far honour all men reaches is a real division. Robertson qualifies it at once — "not with the same honour" — Barnes reads it as respect "due to them according to their personal worth, and to the rank and office which they sustain", Clarke as honour "to whom honour is due". Ellicott takes it as an advance on Paul at that very point: Paul said the honour was for those to whom it was due, but Peter "says that this includes all men; there is not one who can be entirely despised, not one who has quite lost the likeness of Christ". Calvin agrees "none are to be neglected", rejecting the narrowing to rulers since "honor to magistrates is included in the last clause". Wesley grounds the universal reading in three facts: all men are "made in the image of God, bought by his Son, and designed for his kingdom".

Ellicott quotes Leighton on the arrangement of the four commands, the fear of God "set in the middle betwixt these, as the common spring of all duty to men, and the sovereign rule by which it is to be regulated". Robertson notes that the word for brotherhood is "rare save in ecclesiastical literature" but "a word for all Christians", that the fear is meant "in both senses of reverence and dread", and that the verse makes "a fine motto".
18:
The word is not the one Paul uses, and all four say so. Robertson glosses it "house servants (slaves) in distinction from the general term" for slave. Ellicott says it "brings forward the family or household relation of servant or slave to master, and not... the mere fact of ownership", and answers the objection that such directions are odd in a letter to Jewish Christians: "there were large numbers of Hebrews in this position." Calvin explains the choice by exposure: domestics "came more in contact with their masters, and were more liable to be ill-treated".

Barnes presses the distinction into a denial. The word "should not and cannot be employed to prove that slavery existed in the churches to which Peter wrote, and still less to prove that he approved of slavery", applying equally to "persons employed as domestics, though they had voluntarily hired themselves out". Henry states the opposite: "servants in those days generally were slaves, and had heathen masters, who often used them cruelly."

Gill supplies the objection Peter answers, and it is doctrinal rather than social. The Jews held "that because they were the seed of Abraham, they ought not to be the servants of any"; and believers among them thought they need not serve unbelieving masters, "nor indeed believing ones, because they were equally brethren in Christ".

What kind of fear is meant is guarded from two sides. Ellicott insists "all implies everything which goes to make up true fear", meaning no "unmanly cowardice". Calvin defines it by its opposites: "that sincere and willing reverence, which they acknowledge by their office to be due", set "in opposition to dissimulation as well as to forced subjection", since men who would throw off the yoke if they could "cannot be said properly to fear". His conclusion: "fear arises from a right knowledge of duty." Wesley makes it double: fear "of offending them or God".

On the froward master Clarke is the most practical and startling. The word means "the crooked, perverse, unreasonable morose, and austere", and his counsel divides responsibility: "your time belongs to your master; obey him in every thing that is not sinful; if he employs you about unreasonable or foolish things, let him answer for it. He may waste your time... you can only fill up your time." Henry states the principle as a rule: "the sinful misconduct of one relation, does not justify sinful behaviour in the other" — adding, against the drift of the passage, that "masters should be meek and gentle".

The phrase rendered thankworthy is literally "this is grace", and has a controversial history. Ellicott reports that "some of the older Roman Catholic divines pressed it into the service of the supererogation theory", reading it as "this deserves grace as its reward", and dismisses it: "it is needless to point out how shallow a view of duty is implied in the thought that it was more than duty to be thus submissive."

Barnes rules out the obvious English sense: it "does not mean that it was worthy of thanks, or that God would thank them for doing it... but that such conduct would meet with his approbation". Calvin takes it as praise, comparing the Hebrew idiom of finding favour with God. Robertson objects on lexical grounds — "acceptable calls for" a different Greek word, "not the text here" — and states the condition exactly: "suffering is not a blessing in and of itself, but, if one's duty to God is involved, then one can meet it with gladness of heart."

Two explain why the assurance was needed. Calvin notes that "the condition of servants was very hard: they were counted no better than cattle. Such indignity might have driven them to despair." Clarke, following Macknight, finds a principle: obligations depend not "on the character of the person" served "but on the unalterable relations of things established by God".
20:
Ellicott hears the opening question as a joke. The noun is "a poetical and pagan-sounding word, not elsewhere found in the New Testament", so "the sense may be said to be slightly humorous": "if you make a blunder (such is the meaning of fault here — it might include such things as the breaking of dishes), and receive a buffet for it (or a box on the ear — a common punishment of slaves for trifling faults), and bear it with fortitude, do you expect to be made the subject of an heroic or dithyrambic poem?" Robertson catches the same register in three words — "what price glory?" — and draws the moral: "no posing as a martyr allowed here."

Clarke reads the buffeting differently: the Christian slaves "were buffeted because they were Christians, and because they would not join with their masters in idolatrous worship" — not for blunders. Barnes stays with the word, which means "to strike with the fist": such servants "would be likely to be struck in sudden anger, either by the hand, or by anything that was accessible".

Calvin raises the objection the verse invites. When God punishes our sins, "patience is certainly a sacrifice of sweet odour to him", so how can Peter deny it glory? His answer: "Peter does not here speak simply but comparatively; for it is a small and slender praise to bear with submission a just punishment, in comparison with that of an innocent man, who willingly bears the wrongs of men, only because he fears God."

Both close readers object to the English of the second half: Ellicott calls it "a pity that the translators have limited St. Peter's meaning by the insertion of the last two words", and Robertson notes there is "no for it in the Greek here".

The next verse carries a textual variant all three report and none thinks decisive. Clarke says "many MSS. and most of the versions" read for you rather than for us, a reading "which I think is genuine"; Barnes agrees "the latest editions of the Greek Testament adopt" it, though "the sense, however, is not essentially varied".

What they were called to is put more sharply than the English suggests. Robertson says they were called "to suffer without flinching", Christ's suffering lifting theirs "to a new plane". Ellicott takes the calling back to their evangelisation: "it was a special point in St. Paul's preaching to forewarn fairly of the tribulations attending all who wished to enter the kingdom of God", so persecution "ought not to be a surprise". He finds a premise hidden in the connective: "notice what a fine assumption lies in this because — that Christ's experience must needs be that of every Christian." Clarke puts it bluntly: "ye cannot expect to fare better than your master."

Calvin refuses to keep the passage among the servants: it "ought not to be confined to that subject", since Peter "reminds all the godly in common as to what the condition of Christianity is". His consolation is comparative: "nothing seems more unworthy, and therefore less tolerable, than undeservedly to suffer; but when we turn our eyes to the Son of God, this bitterness is mitigated; for who would refuse to follow him going before us?"

The word for example is the tile's best philology, and the three agree. Barnes calls it "a writing copy, such as is set for children; or an outline or sketch for a painter to fill up"; Calvin, "a copy set before scholars to be imitated"; Robertson supplies the ancient evidence, Clement of Alexandria using it "of the copy-head at the top of a child's exercise book... including all the letters of the alphabet". Barnes cautions against pressing it: Peter "does not say that this was the only object for which Christ suffered, but that it was an object, and an important one".
22:
Ellicott insists the verse be read forward: "it is not the sinlessness of Christ by itself that is here set as an example before the servants, but His sinlessness in combination with His ill-treatment, or rather, His meekness under the combination." He then notices a substitution in the quotation from Isaiah: the prophet's word "was one of violent transgression", but Peter replaces it with the mild word he had just used of a servant's blunder, so the sense is "who never made a fault — such as household servants were often committing", the second clause referring likewise to "petty acts of dishonesty, and petty deceits to screen themselves from punishment".

Clarke reaches that explanation of the guile independently: it is mentioned "because those who do wrong generally strive to screen themselves by prevarication and lies". Wesley makes the pairing occupational: the example "is peculiarly adapted to the state of servants, who easily slide either into sin or guile, reviling their fellowservants, or threatening them — the natural result of anger without power". Robertson notes the second clause combines Isaiah with Zephaniah: "Christ's guilelessness stood the test of scrutiny."

Gill states the paradox flatly. Christ "was in the likeness of sinful flesh", was "traduced as a sinner by his enemies, and had all the sins of his people on him" — "but he had no sin in his nature, nor did he commit any in his life". Barnes lists the charges: "accused of being a seditious man; spoken of as a deceiver; charged with being in league with Beelzebub" — answering only that "justice might be done". Calvin turns that against any reader who thinks himself hard done by: "if any one boasts of his own innocence, he must know that Christ did not suffer as a malefactor", and since James makes the man who offends not in his tongue perfect, "no one of us can dare claim" it. Barnes adds the double duty: "it is as much our duty to live so as not to deserve the reproaches of others, as it is to bear them with patience."

Ellicott returns the scene to the servants' quarters. Reviling was what slaves were "particularly liable to", and "instances are not wanting in the comic poets where they lose their self-control under it, and openly rate their owners in return". The suffering "implies actual bodily maltreatment", to which they "could not answer directly by striking in return, but would sometimes take their revenge by threats — run away, or burn the house, or poison the food".

Robertson reads the verse through its tenses. The verbs for reviling and threatening are imperfects "for repeated incidents", the compound for answering abuse "late and rare... here only in N.T.", its prefix meaning "in turn, return". The last verb is imperfect too — "kept on committing himself" — and he insists on the object: not another, "as the Sanhedrin" did, "but himself".

Clarke reports a variant that changes the sentence: the Vulgate and some Latin fathers read "he delivered himself to him who judged unrighteously", meaning Pilate — "some critics approve of this reading, but it has not sufficient evidence to recommend it as genuine". Calvin keeps the received text: Peter adds the clause so that those who "patiently endured the reproaches and violence of the wicked" should know "they would have God as their defender".

Cyril of Jerusalem turns the verses into a list of charges Christ could not have faced. He was not led to death "for covetousness, since He was a Teacher of poverty"; "not for smiting or striking hastily, for He turned the other cheek also to the smiter; not for despising the Law, for He was the fulfiller of the Law; not for reviling a prophet, for it was Himself who was proclaimed by the Prophets" — then quotes this passage entire, ending "who came to His passion, not unwillingly, but willing".
24:
Ellicott denies that the verse continues the argument from example: it "is intended to make the readers feel the claims of gratitude, not to set before them another point in which Christ was to be imitated". It still reinforces the earlier points: Christ "actually His own self bore ours", "in His own body, so that He could sympathise with the corporal chastisements of these poor servants; and on the tree, too, the wicked slave's death". Wesley says the same, the cross being that "whereon chiefly slaves or servants were wont to suffer".

Clarke's first note answers an ancient error: "his own self" means "not another in his place, as some anciently supposed, because they thought it impossible that the Christ should suffer". Barnes takes the phrase sacrificially — "he did not make expiation by offering a bloody victim, but was himself the sacrifice" — and Robertson supplies the verb, the common word "of bringing sacrifice to the altar", with Bigg: "here St. Peter puts the Cross in the place of the altar."

How the sins were borne is where they part, sharply. Gill takes the load at its widest: Christ bore "all sorts of sin, original and actual", and "all that is in sin... the demerit of it, as both filth, guilt, and punishment". Barnes argues from an impossibility to a substitution: it "cannot mean that Christ so took upon himself the sins of men as to become himself a sinner", so "he put himself in the place of sinners, and bore that which those sins deserved" — "he was treated as if he had been a sinner, in order that we might be treated as if we had not sinned".

Clarke states the negative far more violently. Christ "bore the punishment due to our sins. In no other sense could Christ bear them. To say that they were so imputed to him as if they had been his own, and that the Father beheld him as blackened with imputed sin, is monstrous, if not blasphemous." Wesley agrees in a phrase — "that is, the punishment due to them" — while Calvin keeps the sacrificial frame: "as under the Law, the sinner, that he might be released from guilt, substituted a victim in his own place; so Christ took on himself the curse due to our sins."

Calvin numbers what the verse does, against reading it as example only, which "would have been very frigid": "that Christ by his death has given us an example of patience"; "that by his death he restored us to life"; and "that we, being dead to sins, ought to live to righteousness" — the middle obliging us to follow the first.

The philology is contested at a preposition. Ellicott reports that "most modern scholars are agreed to reject on the tree, in favour of the marginal to", the proper sense being what colloquial English calls "on-to the tree". Robertson traces the noun: "originally just wood, then something made of wood, as a gibbet or cross". Of the participle he notes an old compound meaning "to get away from", "here only in N.T."; Clarke renders it "being freed from sin — delivered out of its power", so "that righteousness should be our master now, as sin was before".

Wesley closes the antithesis with a count: righteousness "is one only. The sins we had committed, and he bore, were manifold." Clarke, still addressing servants "scourged, buffeted, and variously maltreated", keeps the healing in the register of the stripes: what is healed is "the deep and inveterate wounds, inflicted on their souls by sin". Cyril of Jerusalem sets it as a dilemma resolved: "either that God, in His truth, should destroy all men, or that in His loving-kindness He should cancel the sentence. But behold the wisdom of God; He preserved both the truth of His sentence, and the exercise of His loving-kindness."
25:
The first thing corrected is the grammar. Ellicott holds that "the right reading does not attach going astray to sheep, but as predicate of the sentence, ye were going astray like sheep", and Robertson agrees, calling it a periphrastic imperfect with a present participle meaning "to wander away". Ellicott also fixes the connective: the "for" explains "how they came to be in need of healing", and he paraphrases — "I may well say that ye were healed; for Israelites though you are, your consciences and memories tell you that you were as far gone in wilful error as any Gentiles, and needed as complete a conversion."

He then admits a defect in the writing and excuses it. "The two metaphors, of healing and going astray, do not match very well, but the fact that both are quotations from Isaiah makes their disagreement less harsh" — adding that one sees "how deeply that prophecy... had sunk into St. Peter's mind", its interpretation "probably learned from the Baptist".

Calvin locates the emphasis elsewhere. On the word sheep "there is no particular stress"; the weight falls on what the prophet adds, "that every one had turned to his own way", so that "we are all going astray from the way of salvation, and proceeding in the way of ruin, until Christ brings us back". Ellicott gets the same universality differently: "Jew and Gentile take different ways, but both alike fulfil the prophecy, every man to his own way".

Gill treats the title sheep as a problem rather than a compliment. God's elect are sheep before conversion — "not that they have the agreeable properties of sheep, as to be meek, harmless, innocent, clean, and profitable, for they are the reverse of all this", nor because they are "unprejudiced against, and predisposed unto the Gospel". They are sheep "in electing grace", by the Father's gift, and only afterwards by hearing and following. Barnes keeps the figure descriptive: "we were like a flock without a shepherd... without a protector, and were exposed to every kind of danger".

Clarke turns the point on the readers' situation: they "were not in a better moral condition than your oppressors" — the servants addressed throughout are told their masters' vices had been theirs — until Christ "called you back from your wanderings, by sending you the Gospel of his grace".

On the tense of the return Ellicott is precise: the verb "points to the actual historical time at which it took place, rather than the position now occupied", so "but now ye returned". Calvin would render the clause "but you have been now restored... to the shepherd and the bishop of your souls", and concludes that "all who are not ruled by Christ, are wandering like lost sheep in the ways of error" — by which "is condemned the whole wisdom of the world".

The second title provokes the most comment. Barnes glosses it "overseer", a word applicable "to one who inspects or oversees anything, as public works, or the execution of treaties", or "an inspector of wares offered for sale"; Wesley calls him "the kind observer, inspector, or overseer of your souls". Clarke insists on the translation and then on its consequence: unless the English word is understood as the Greek overseer, "it can convey to us no meaning of the original" — and since Christ "is still supreme Bishop or Overseer in his Church", he alone is "Episcopus episcoporum, the Bishop of bishops; a title which the Romish pontiffs have blasphemously usurped".

Robertson observes that this is the only place where Christ is so called, and that "Philo calls God" by the same word, both titles being combined in Ezekiel. Calvin reports the same identification, the shepherd title marking Christ as the figure foretold there and the overseer title alluding to the promise "I will oversee them".
